newsitem.title: USA: MSRB issues new interpretation of pay-to-play rule.
newsitem.headline: MSRB issues new interpretation of pay-to-play rule.

text.p: Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board on Friday had good news and bad news for bond underwriters in a new interpretation of its "pay-to-play" rule G-37.

The board ruled that dealers that are banned from doing business with particular issuers because of "pay-to-play" violations, can nevertheless continue work on certain pending deals with those localities if bond purchase agreements were signed before contributions were made.

"For example, if a bond purchase agreement was signed prior to the date of the contribution, a dealer may continue to perform its services as an underwriter," financial adviser, remarketing or placement agent, or underwriter of commercial paper, the board said.

Meanwhile, the board also said that dealers that have certain ongoing contracts with issuers that allow for "additional services or compensation" for deals covered by G-37 bans, could not provide those supplemental services.
For example, a dealer may have an remarketing agreement that lets the issuer change the "mode" of the outstanding bonds from a variable to fixed rate of interest, the board said.
Such provisions in existing contracts would be "new" muni securities business and, therefore, barred under G-37, MSRB said.

MSRB's interpretation stems, in part, from a recent Massachusetts Water Resources Authority decision not to replace Morgan Stanley & Co. as co-manager of the authority's commercial paper program following an employee's improper contribution under rule G-37.
According to a report in Financial Markets Daily, MWRA officials were waiting for Friday's MSRB interpretation before deciding whether to keep Morgan Stanley on board.
Christopher Taylor, MSRB's executive director, said MWRA could keep Morgan Stanley as co-manager under the existing contract as long as the firm does not get any more compensaton.
Enacted in April 1994, rule G-37 prohibits muni dealers that make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments.
The 15-member board also said on Friday that dealers that signed long-term contracts to provide broad services to issuers before giving an improper contribution, may not continue with the agreements.
An example is a five-year pact to provide financial advisory services, the board said.

"The board is not going to tolerate a situation where someone says I'm thinking about doing a GO deal in two years. When I finish up on that I'll terminate my relationship," MSRB's Taylor said in a telephone interview.
MSRB said issuers have a transition period under the interpretation to find new professionals. The period should be as short as possible, the board noted.

MSRB's interpretation is now in effect, but the board asked for comments. There are a lot of different agreements out there, and the interpretation may not deal with all of them adequately, the board said.
The panel said, in particular, it wants further examples of how a dealer may be contractually obligated to perform certain tasks after a G-37 ban is triggered.
Taylor said Friday's interpretation reiterates the board's "very strong view that noone should benefit from having made a contribution to someone in a position to give them business."
He stressed, however, that industry compliance with rule G-37 has been "outstanding." He said there have been less than two dozen instances of G-37 bans.
